executiveSummary: A neighborhood group asks the city council's transportation committee to fund a twelve-week protected-lane pilot on Harmon Avenue, the city's most dangerous crossing, for less than a year of crash cleanup.

slides.slideTitle: Harmon Avenue can be safe by summer
slides.subtitle: Transportation committee · March 4 · Harmon Neighbors
slides.speakerNotes:
- Thank you for the time this evening.
- I'm Dana Ruiz. I live two blocks from Harmon and 9th, and I'm here about that one intersection and one vote.

slides.slideTitle: Harmon and 9th had more crashes last year than any crossing in the city
keyBullets: 23 crashes at Harmon and 9th in 2025
Up from 14 in 2022
Source: city police crash reports
slides.speakerNotes:
- That figure is from your own police reports, not ours.
- It is the highest in the city for the second year running, and it has gone up every year since the bus route moved onto Harmon.
- Nine of the twenty-three involved someone on a bike or on foot.

slides.slideTitle: The crossing guard has stopped three near misses since September
keyBullets: “I hold my sign up and I still watch cars go around me.”
Marta Diaz, crossing guard at Harmon and 9th since 2017
slides.speakerNotes:
- Marta has worked that corner for eight years. She asked me to read you this.
- Three times this school year she has pulled a child back onto the curb.
- She is not asking for a new job. She is asking for a street that does part of hers.
slides.intent: Put a face on the number

slides.slideTitle: Beacon Street cut injury crashes by more than half with the same design
keyBullets: Before: 31 injury crashes a year
After: 12 a year, three years running
Source: Somerville traffic report, 2024
slides.speakerNotes:
- This is not a guess. Somerville put a protected lane on Beacon Street in 2021, with the same posts and paint we are asking for.
- Injury crashes fell from thirty-one a year to twelve, and they stayed there.
- Their traffic engineer has offered to brief your staff.

slides.slideTitle: A twelve-year-old could ride to Lincoln Middle School on Harmon by June
keyBullets: 1.4 miles, one turn, every crossing signaled
slides.speakerNotes:
- Picture the ride. A seventh grader leaves Elm Street, rides Harmon behind a row of posts, and turns at the light on 9th.
- Today no parent on our block lets their kid do that.
- With the lane, forty families on our survey say they would.

slides.slideTitle: The lane takes 38 parking spaces, on blocks that are 60% full at the busiest hour
keyBullets: Spaces removed: 38, all on the east side
Peak use on those blocks: 60%, city count, October
Nearest open lot: the library, 120 spaces, half empty
slides.speakerNotes:
- I want to be straight about the cost to drivers, because you will hear about it.
- Thirty-eight spaces go. The city's own October count found those blocks sixty percent full at peak.
- The library lot a block away is half empty most evenings.

slides.slideTitle: The pilot costs less than one year of crash response on Harmon
keyBullets: $84,000 for the twelve-week pilot
$112,000 a year in crash response on Harmon, city estimate
slides.speakerNotes:
- Eighty-four thousand dollars buys the paint, the posts, and two signal changes.
- Your public works office puts crash response on Harmon at a hundred and twelve thousand a year: police, ambulance, cleanup, repairs.
- The pilot pays for itself if it prevents a few months of that.
slides.intent: Make the price small beside the problem

slides.slideTitle: The pilot runs twelve weeks, and the counts are public every Friday
keyBullets: Week 1: paint, posts, signal timing
Weeks 2–11: crash and traffic counts every Monday, posted each Friday
Week 12: report to this committee
slides.speakerNotes:
- We are not asking you to trust us. We are asking you to watch.
- Staff count crashes and traffic every Monday, and the numbers go on the city's site every Friday.
- In week twelve, you get a report and decide.
slides.intent: Make the step small and visible

slides.slideTitle: If the pilot fails, the posts come out in a day
keyBullets: The posts are bolted, not poured
Taking them out costs $6,000
No concrete until the counts say so
slides.speakerNotes:
- If the numbers don't move, you lose very little.
- The posts bolt down. Public works can pull them in a day for six thousand dollars.
- Concrete waits until the counts earn it.

slides.slideTitle: Vote Tuesday to fund the pilot
keyBullets: Fund $84,000 from the street safety reserve
Paint in April, report in July
Judge it on one number: crashes at Harmon and 9th
slides.speakerNotes:
- Here is the ask, plainly.
- Fund the pilot from the street safety reserve on Tuesday, so the paint goes down in April.
- Then judge it on one number in July. If it's not lower, pull the posts.

slides.slideTitle: For less than a year of cleanup, Harmon and 9th can stop being the city's worst crossing
slides.subtitle: Fund the pilot on Tuesday
slides.speakerNotes:
- Twenty-three crashes last year. Marta on the curb with her sign.
- Or a seventh grader riding to school behind a row of posts, for less than the city already spends cleaning up.
- Thank you. I'm glad to take questions.
